title: Impairment of Performance Variables After In-Season Strength-Training Cessation in Elite Cyclists
authors: Rønnestad BR, Hansen J, Hollan I, Spencer M, Ellefsen S
journal: International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance
population: 14 elite cyclists (VO2max 77 +/- 6 and 73 +/- 5 mL/kg/min) randomised to 25 weeks of endurance plus heavy strength training (n = 7) or endurance only (n = 7), then 8 weeks of endurance only for both. Cyclists, not runners.
findings: The strength group trained 3 x 4-10RM, 1 to 2 days a week for 25 weeks, then both groups trained endurance only for 8 weeks at the start of the competition season.

During the 25 weeks the strength group had larger gains than the control group in maximal isometric half-squat force, squat jump, maximal aerobic power, power at 4 mmol/L lactate and mean power in a 30-second Wingate test (ES 0.46-0.74).
During the 8 weeks without strength training the strength group lost squat jump height, maximal aerobic power and Wingate mean power relative to the control group (ES 0.49-0.84).

The authors read this as a rapid decline of the adaptations on termination of strength training in the first 8 weeks of the competition period in elite cyclists. Data were assessed by magnitude-based inferences.
limitations: Seven cyclists per group, elite cyclists and not runners, and a magnitude-based inference analysis; the lifting dose was 1 to 2 days a week and the stop lasted 8 weeks. The abstract does not state the absolute losses. Abstract read; full text not read.
implications: After 8 weeks without strength work the strength group of elite cyclists lost squat jump height, maximal aerobic power and Wingate power relative to the control group, so a long gap in lifting may not be harmless in a different sport. It is a reason for the plan to keep one light session through the specific phase and the taper as a default, not as a requirement.
The runners' result over 4 weeks points the other way (berryman-2020-strength-cessation-runners); the two differ in sport, length of stop and type of training, and neither tests a taper.
